debate.situation: Three new skincare products went on last week, and your face now stings. You know the timing and the symptom; you don't yet know which product, which ingredient, or whether it is irritation, an allergy, or something unrelated like weather or a changed routine. How the stinging looks (redness, swelling, hives, spreading) and whether it eases when you stop are the decisive unknowns.

minds.title: The Experimenter
minds.concern: Isolating one cause through controlled, one-change-at-a-time testing.
minds.author: Claude Bernard
minds.book: An Introduction to the Study of Experimental Medicine

minds.title: The Story Skeptic
minds.concern: Guarding against a tidy but wrong explanation built from thin evidence.
minds.author: Daniel Kahneman

minds.title: The Subtractor
minds.concern: Removing possible harms first, before adding anything new.
minds.author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb

debate.speaker: The Experimenter
debate.text: Stop all three, let your face settle, then reintroduce them one at a time, a few days apart. Whichever one brings the sting back is your suspect. Testing all three together tells you nothing about who did it.
debate.author: Claude Bernard
debate.book: An Introduction to the Study of Experimental Medicine
debate.basis: Basis: Claude Bernard, An Introduction to the Study of Experimental Medicine (1865). Source not verified; no link or section given.

debate.speaker: The Subtractor
debate.text: Before reintroducing anything, I'd go further: strip your routine to a gentle cleanser and plain moisturizer. Your skin may be irritated by the pile-up, not one villain. Removing things is cheap and low-risk. Adding things back is where new trouble can start.
debate.author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb
debate.basis: Basis: Nassim Nicholas Taleb, Antifragile, his idea of via negativa (improving by subtraction). Source not verified; no link given.

debate.speaker: The Story Skeptic
debate.text: Careful, both of you. The newest product is the obvious suspect, and that is exactly why I distrust it. A neat story feels true because it is neat. Did the weather change? A new pillowcase? Sun? We may be blaming the wrong thing.
debate.author: Daniel Kahneman
debate.basis: Basis: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow, on how the mind favors coherent stories over missing evidence. Source not verified; no link given.

debate.speaker: The Experimenter
debate.text: Fair, and that's why I want a control. If the stinging fades once the products stop but nothing else changes, the products gain weight. If it persists, your alternatives get stronger. Your story-doubt is just another reason to test cleanly.
debate.author: Claude Bernard
debate.book: An Introduction to the Study of Experimental Medicine
debate.basis: Basis: Claude Bernard, An Introduction to the Study of Experimental Medicine (1865). Source not verified; no link or section given.

debate.speaker: The Subtractor
debate.text: Then the pause is the experiment's first step, and I'd keep it long enough. Skin recovers slowly. Reintroducing after one calm day may just reproduce the irritation and teach us little. Patience here protects the data and the skin.
debate.author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb
debate.basis: Basis: Nassim Nicholas Taleb, Antifragile, via negativa. Source not verified; no link given.

debate.speaker: The Story Skeptic
debate.text: Agreed on patience, but watch for another trap: you will be watching your face closely, and anyone staring at a mirror finds something. Note redness and sting in a short daily log, and judge it before you know which product was reintroduced, if possible.
debate.author: Daniel Kahneman
debate.basis: Basis: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow, on attention and biased judgment. Source not verified; no link given.

debate.speaker: The Experimenter
debate.text: A log is good, but be honest about limits. Ingredients interact, and a product might only irritate when combined with another, or when the skin barrier is already weak. One-at-a-time testing can miss that. Retest the suspect alone, then paired, if the result is unclear.
debate.author: Claude Bernard
debate.book: An Introduction to the Study of Experimental Medicine
debate.basis: Basis: Claude Bernard, An Introduction to the Study of Experimental Medicine (1865). Source not verified; no link or section given.

debate.speaker: The Subtractor
debate.text: And my own rule has a limit too: subtraction is not always safe. If you see swelling, hives, blistering, or trouble breathing, don't experiment at all. Wash it off and get medical help. Some signals mean stop testing and ask a professional.
debate.author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb
debate.basis: Basis: Nassim Nicholas Taleb, Antifragile, his caution about avoiding severe downside. The medical warning is my own addition, not Taleb's claim. Source not verified; no link given.

debate.speaker: The Story Skeptic
debate.text: That settles one disagreement for me. I wanted to doubt the product theory, but with a severe reaction I'd act on the simplest explanation first. For mild stinging, I'd still keep the other causes open until the pause shows what changes.
debate.author: Daniel Kahneman
debate.basis: Basis: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow, on weighing intuitive stories against evidence. Source not verified; no link given.

debate.speaker: The Experimenter
debate.text: Then here's where we stand: pause, watch, log, reintroduce slowly, and treat any single result as provisional. We still differ on how fast to retest, but not on the principle that one clean change beats three muddled ones.
debate.author: Claude Bernard
debate.book: An Introduction to the Study of Experimental Medicine
debate.basis: Basis: Claude Bernard, An Introduction to the Study of Experimental Medicine (1865). Source not verified; no link or section given.

debate.clearer: The main insight is that the question is less 'which product is it?' and more 'how can I learn that without guessing or making it worse?' Pausing first, logging changes, and reintroducing one product at a time all serve that. Still disputed: how long to wait before retesting, and how much weight to give non-product causes like weather or sun. A possible self-reflection: what else changed in your routine or environment that week? None of the three minds can diagnose you, and the book sources cited here were not verified against the texts.
debate.dependsOn: If you see swelling, hives, blistering, or trouble breathing, or the sting is severe, stopping everything and getting medical help is more reasonable than testing, because those can signal an allergic or serious reaction. If the stinging is mild and fades within days of pausing the products, a slow one-at-a-time reintroduction becomes reasonable, because it can point to the culprit. If the stinging continues after a couple of weeks off all three, an unrelated cause becomes more likely, and a dermatologist or pharmacist can help, perhaps with patch testing. If you don't know whether a product shares an ingredient with something you have reacted to before, checking the ingredient lists against past reactions is a proportionate way to find out.
